newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Olivetti's Caio faces fresh probe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Olivetti's Caio faces fresh probe.

text.p: Francesco Caio, chief executive of crisis-hit Olivetti, faces a further grilling this time by magistrates from the company's home time of Ivrea on the group's finances, causing its share price on Monday to slump.

Caio, who has headed the loss-making information technology group for just over 10 turbulent weeks, will be questioned in a preliminary probe into the group's accounts by magistrates from the north-western town near Turin, said judicial sources.

The questioning is the first step of an investigation which could lead to a full-scale criminal inquiry into statements made by the struggling group on its financial accounts and follows a similar probe by stock market watchdog authority Consob.

The move unnerved Olivetti shares which fell to a record low of 515 lire before being automatically suspended by the Milan bourse for falling the 10 percent limit-down. After a failed attempt to restart trading, the shares remained suspended. Ivrea magistrates, who launched their inquiry at the weekend, have questioned former Olivetti director-general in charge of finance and auditing, Renzo Francesconi, after he cast doubts on the accuracy of the group's first half accounts.

Olivetti stock began to slide earlier in the day after the group cancelled anxiously awaited analysts' meetings this week and delayed the publication of its fully detailed first-half 1996 results until the end of this month.

Late on Friday, Olivetti called off the analysts meetings in Milan on Monday and London on Tuesday as the crisis-hit group attempted to satisfy an earlier investigation by stock market watchdog Consob over its financial accounts.

Earlier this month, Olivetti reported initial first half 1996 results showing sales sliding, losses continuing and debts deepening. Francesconi resigned a day later after he questioned the validity of the group's financial figures.

Financial analysts said the group must produce a full set of approved accounts before the process of re-building confidence in the group can start. Market talk that the group's debts were worse than reported had already prompted selling of the shares.
Olivetti has recorded losses for the last five years and seems set to make it six years after reporting a 440.2 billion lire ($290 million) loss in the first six months of 1996.

Its new businesss of mobile and fixed line telephone networks continue to absorb cash while its older core business of personal computers, office equipment and computer systems falter under stiff competitive pressures.

Foreign funds invested heavily in Olivetti as part of the group's 2.257 trillion lire rights issue a year ago and these overseas shareholders, holding 70 percent of Olivetti, have been demanding more financial information from the group.
"The financial position is crucial, and some clarity of the debt level is urgently needed," said one industry analyst.

Analysts are looking for some light to be shed on how the group will continue to fund investment in its expanding telephony business and pay for group restructuring while its older core businesses falter. ($1=1,522 lire)
